speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore's continued success depends very much on our ability to remain a vibrant international business and commercial hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In a world that is at risk of turning inward, we have doubled down on our commitment to remain open and connected to the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We welcome the best companies from around the world to be sited in Singapore – bring their base into Singapore and do their business in, from, or out of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also encourage and support our own companies to pursue regional or even global ambitions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can only work by ensuring that the business environment is facilitative of cross-border transactions and activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has not changed our approach, but has made it even more imperative that we remain open and connected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Acceding to the Apostille Convention is a step in pursuit of this commitment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It signals in concrete terms to the international community that Singapore remains open for business.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, a person seeking to relocate or study abroad may need to produce identification documents, academic transcripts, proof of residency, proof of employment or income and other such similar supporting documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Businesses seeking to acquire properties overseas may need to produce incorporation documents and also produce official business profiles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many states require that foreign public documents be “legalised” before they are recognised and accepted in those states.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whilst differences exist amongst states, the process of “legalisation” typically involves the authentication of the signature, the seal or the stamp on a local public document by a series of different public officials along a “chain”, examining the document and reviewing at each step the different aspects of legalisation, where the ultimate authentication is recognised by the state of destination.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is oftentimes cumbersome and costly, and not to mention time-consuming as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Apostille Convention replaces the process of “legalisation” with a one-step process involving a single certificate issued by the state’s designated Competent Authority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will be in good company: there are 118 Contracting Parties to the Apostille Convention, including some of Singapore’s major trading partners such as the USA, the UK, India and the EU member states.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Acceding to the Apostille Convention bolsters Singapore's reputation as a bustling and interconnected hub, and will serve as a statement of Singapore's intent to remain committed as a global player in facilitating international movements, transactions and activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will save cost and time for persons who seek to use Singapore-issued public documents in other Contracting Parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Likewise, Singapore's authorities will be obliged to accept apostilles in place of legalisation for incoming foreign public documents from other Contracting Parties, where applicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The purposes of the Bill are fairly straightforward and are three-fold.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the Bill provides for apostilles to be issued for Singapore public documents by Singapore's Competent Authority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Presently, MFA performs the legalisation function in respect of outgoing documents issued out of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This function is needed for outgoing public documents intended for use in Contracting Parties with legalisation requirements, until Singapore becomes a Party to the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This function will continue to be needed for outgoing public documents intended for use in non-Contracting Parties with legalisation requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The legalisation and apostillisation functions will thereafter be centralised in one agency – this is of course more user-friendly and also efficient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 21(2) of the Bill therefore transfers the legalisation function from MFA to SAL.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The transfer of the legalisation function from MFA to SAL ties in with SAL's current authentication services, making it more convenient for the legal industry and the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, clause 9 of the Bill expressly exempts public documents executed in other Contracting Parties from any requirement of legalisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our written laws do not currently require incoming foreign public documents to be legalised, before they are recognised and accepted in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As an administrative practice, however, some agencies would require foreign documents to be so legalised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the Bill, Government agencies may no longer require such foreign documents to be legalised if the documents come from a Contracting Party to the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In its place, these agencies may require the apostilles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the Bill provides for the effect of apostilles issued by other Contracting Parties and facilitates, but does not require, their use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The apostille does not, however, certify the contents of the underlying public document; neither is this the position for legalisation as well today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also provides for the effect of apostilles, so as to facilitate their use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that for foreign public documents which Government agencies do not require to be legalised, apostilles may not subsequently be required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The rationale behind this is to ensure that agencies do not take a regressive step by requiring the formality of an apostille, when previously there had been no other formality requirements needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, apostilles may be required for new classes of foreign public documents created after Singapore's accession to the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Bill also contains a related amendment to the Evidence Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact is, that the topic of legalisation of public documents is hardly something that will excite one's senses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, on the other hand, am feeling elated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because, I suggested in this House that Singapore ratify the Apostille Convention by way of a Parliamentary Question that came up for answer in this House on 20 November 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, the hon Minister for Law informed this House that the Government was looking into this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: About two years later, the Apostille Bill is presented in this House for consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst the subject matter of this Bill may be boring, it is one that can have positive impact for Singaporeans as outlined by the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It seems to me that it is not working.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Never mind Sir, in the interest of time, I will just proceed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I was about to show the legalisation process, but thankfully, the hon Minister had outlined the legalisation process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Without the Apostille Convention, there are four, possibly five stages, which are required to be undergone before the document in the state of origin, is recognised in the state of destination.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That, as the hon Minister mentioned, translates to enormous savings of time and costs because you no longer have to go to the consulate authority to have the documents legalised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, Singaporeans would get the benefit of the convention to have their vital documents issued by public authorities recognised in these countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These documents include birth certificates, marriage certificates and death certificates It also, as the hon Minister mentioned, strengthen Singapore's a attraction as a premier business and international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is because, oversees public documents can also be readily recognised here, for business purposes as well as for legal proceedings here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, plainly there are many positives about this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: While Singapore may be a relatively late adopter of the Apostille Convention, it has an opportunity to be a leader in the digitalisation of the apostille process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Particularly in respect to two areas, e-Apostille and e-Registers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The e-Apostille system enables Singaporeans to apply for a public document to be issued with an e-Apostille system online.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hopefully this can be done via SingPass in the near future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The e-Register system will enable a person to verify online the authenticity of an apostille issued by the Competent Authority, in this case, it is the Singapore Academy of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is plain to see how beneficial the digitalisation of the apostille processes will be for the users of this systems.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The processes would be made more secure, efficient and of course environment-friendly too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister’s view on my suggestion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I also have a query with respect to fees that will be charged for issuance of the apostille by the Singapore Academy of Law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I note that MFA currently charges $10 for the legalisation of each document.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, there is a wide range from as low as one Euro to as high as 70 Euros.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For the Apostille process to be cost-effective for fellow Singaporeans, the fee imposed should also be reasonable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wonder whether the hon Minister will be able to guide us in this area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I daresay that save for practising lawyers and to be fair, the hon Member Mr Louis Ng who would be speaking after me, not many would have heard of the Apostille Convention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, many Members were asking about this in the Members' Room earlier today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The vast majority of backbencher Members of Parliament on both sides of this House are not full-time Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Having a House of backbencher Members of Parliament, not of professional politicians but each of us holding different areas of knowledge and expertise ensures that we, as a House, do not have the same blind spots.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Combined with a listening frontbench, we will be able to make better contributions to policy-making for Singapore and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will significantly cut down on bureaucratic processes, which I think we can all agree, is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I just have four points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the criteria for disproving certified documents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 11 of the Bill provides that the origin of a foreign public document certified with an Apostille will be presumed to be "sufficiently proven" unless "the contrary is proven".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The origin of a foreign public document, as Minister mentioned, is defined in section 7 as comprising three elements: the authenticity of signature, the capacity of the person signing and the identity of the seal or stamp.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify whether problems with just one element of the origin, such as the authenticity of the signature, is enough to cause the origins of the document to be insufficiently proven?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the scope of verification that will be done by the Singapore Academy of Law or SAL before issuing an apostille.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Generally, SAL is only supposed to authenticate the origin of the public document and not whether the document is valid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, defects in the document’s validity may mean the document does not qualify as a public document.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share whether SAL will verify that the document complies with content and format requirements to qualify as a public document?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on apostille fraud which is a problem within the international apostille system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One example of apostille fraud is using an apostille to legitimise a fake document.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be done, for instance, to legitimise a fake academic certificate issued by a degree mill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are existing offences for forging documents or providing false information to a public servant, which potentially may cover instances of apostille fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, apostille fraud is arguably even more serious given that it undermines the integrity of Singapore's systems on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the Apostilles Convention itself does not provide for any penalties, the Apostilles Handbook makes clear that sanctions may be provided for by domestic law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share the rationale for deciding not to introduce specific offences for apostille fraud under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An e-Apostille is an apostille that is issued in electronic format with an electronic signature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An e-Register on the other hand is a register of apostilles that is kept in electronic form and which is accessible online by the recipient of the Apostille.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 has restricted cross-border mobility but individuals still have to get their foreign public documents authenticated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The e-Apostille and e-Register system have provided a convenient way to get around this problem for many other countries, such as Brazil, Bulgaria, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and the US.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, adoption of these systems could also mean there are more opportunities for bad faith actors to interfere.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we are adopting both or either systems, can Minister share what steps will be taken to protect the integrity of the e-Apostilles or e-Registers given that the documents may contain extremely sensitive information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these points, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Before I start, let me first declare my interest as a notary public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And as a notary public myself, I have long wondered why Singapore has hitherto not been a party to the Hague Convention Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents.So, I certainly support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I say this, bearing in mind that in October last year, SAL made it mandatory for all documents requiring notarisation to be accompanied by a notarial certificate which would in turn be required to be authenticated by SAL and there were new mandatory authentication charges chargeable for all documents to be notarised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I am very pleased to be speaking on this suddenly very exciting Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it is exciting because it is the last speech of the day.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, thank you very much, Mr Pillai, for your contributions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, on this question of the e-Apostille and the e-Register.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this would include the issuance of electronic apostilles, and the operation of electronic registers of apostilles that can be accessed online by recipients so that they can verify the paper apostilles or e-Apostilles that they have received and this, I think is the "e-Register” that Mr Ng had in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once this is ready, announcements will be made so that the process can then be explained and it will be known when this can be implemented.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pillai and Mr Tan raised the question of fees that will be charged once SAL takes over.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Members will note that this is the same fee as charged by MFA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to Mr Tan's query earlier, be aswe have sured.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The fee is being charged on the basis that SAL adopts the same manual, over-the-counter authentication services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to note that private documents have to be notarised first before being authenticated by SAL.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the process today anyway, and the apostille fee does not include the cost of such notarisation fees, if applicable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similar to other fees for services, SAL, like any other agencies, will regularly look at its fee structure and will conduct the review at some stage as to whether the fee structure is appropriate for the kind of services that it is designed to support.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked whether if you have one element of the origin of a foreign public document not being satisfied, whether that would vitiate the entire document.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clause 7 provides for three requirements and the three requirements go together to establish the veracity of that document that is being apostillised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if any one element is missing, then a document will not be able to be established.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, Mr Ng would note that, in particular, if the authenticity of the signature cannot be established, then that one fundamental aspect of the document's veracity is cast into doubt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As to Mr Ng's about whether SAL will verify a document that complies with content and format requirements to qualify for a public document, for such Singapore public documents, SAL must be satisfied with the origin of the document before it issues the apostille.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is provided for in clause 17 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SAL will establish very clear procedures for every request for an apostille and is also building up a database of all the public specimen signatures of public officers who are authorised to sign public documents so that there can also be ease of verification.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I should just caution to add to Mr Ng's point that such an apostillisation, like legalisation, does not look at the underlying veracity of the contents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the truth or falsity of the contents of the document is not something that is certified by the apostillisation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng asked about offences for apostille fraud under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is thus not necessary to create a separate set of offences to support only the apostillisation process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng would also note that one of the grounds on which the Competent Authority might refuse to issue an apostille is if there are, itself reasonable grounds, either on the face of it or upon review that the document has been falsified or is otherwise forged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we had extensive consultations with various domestic agencies and also stakeholders to ensure that we are ready with it and that upon accession to the Convention, we will be able to discharge the obligations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have since done so and we are satisfied that we can adopt this regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new regime will modernise and streamline the authentication process and, as I mentioned at the outset, facilitate the use of documents for cross-border purposes, saving time and expense for parties, both ways.
